description: We are developing an interactive, space-themed mission simulator that makes space exploration fun and educational for young learners. Players act as mission commanders, managing a lunar or Martian outpost while balancing oxygen, power, food, and radiation protection. Through challenges, unexpected events, and strategic decisions, they explore the engineering trade-offs of astronaut survival, using science and insights from NASA’s open datasets.
summary:
M-STRONAUT is an interactive, browser-based 3D space exploration and mission simulator that lets players take command of robotic and human exploration missions across the Moon and Mars. Built with Three.js and WebGL, the project uses NASA and Canadian Space Agency resources to introduce planetary terrain, space weather, radiation, subsurface water ice, and other real scientific concepts through interactive missions.
Players explore 3D environments, operate rovers, manage six essential mission resources, and make time-limited engineering decisions where every choice has consequences. A collection of 42 educational science cards connects gameplay to real space missions and discoveries.
By turning complex planetary science and systems engineering challenges into hands-on experiences, M-STRONAUT aims to make space exploration more engaging and understandable for young learners while encouraging scientific curiosity, critical thinking, and problem-solving.
details:
What the project does and how it works

M-STRONAUT is a browser-based 3D planetary exploration and mission simulator. Players take on the role of mission commanders and explore interactive environments across the Moon and Mars. The application uses Three.js and WebGL to render planetary scenes, while modular JavaScript systems manage astronaut movement, rover controls, mission objectives, resource consumption, decision-making, and scoring.

Players monitor six essential mission resources: crew health, oxygen, water, food, base power, and rover battery. During missions, they encounter time-limited engineering decisions in which they must choose between two options with different operational consequences. The simulation enforces a 30% critical resource threshold: if any tracked resource falls below it, the mission enters a failure state. Rover movement also consumes battery, and players must navigate back to designated docking or base locations.

The project includes an educational museum of 33 science cards covering lunar and Martian exploration, real missions, scientific instruments, and planetary discoveries.

Benefits and intended impact

M-STRONAUT makes planetary science and space engineering more interactive and approachable for young learners. Instead of only reading about space missions, players experience the challenges of operating in unfamiliar environments. They learn that scientific exploration involves trade-offs: using more power may improve a survey, but it can reduce the resources available for survival.

The project aims to encourage STEM learning, scientific curiosity, critical thinking, and problem-solving by connecting gameplay decisions with real NASA and Canadian Space Agency missions and scientific resources.

Tools and technologies

  • Programming languages: JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, and CSS3.
  • 3D graphics: Three.js and WebGL.
  • Audio: Browser Web Audio API for procedurally generated sound effects.
  • Development tools: Node.js, Vite, npm, and PowerShell.
  • Data formats: JSON scientific datasets, GeoTIFF/DEM-derived terrain data, and SVG graphics.
  • Persistence: Browser LocalStorage for saving game progression.

Creativity and design considerations

The project combines 3D planetary exploration with resource management and time-limited engineering dilemmas. Its distinctive features include rover route breadcrumbs that help players track their movements, low-gravity movement, environmental and mission-related challenges, and procedural sound effects such as rover motor sounds, radio static, radiation-counter clicks, and warning alerts.

The team considered scientific relevance, resource constraints, usability, and accessibility. The interface uses high-contrast, colorblind-conscious telemetry displays and prominent mission waypoints to help players understand the environment and monitor their resources. The browser-based design also avoids requiring a separate game-engine installation or application download.
